opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think research taste matters so much because the space of possible directions is basically infinite, and your time and compute are not. In machine learning especially, you could spend a whole year on something that's technically interesting and well executed, but it just doesn't end up mattering, because it was solving the wrong problem or the field moved past it.

So taste is really about having a good prior over what's going to be important. It's a sense for which problems are fundamental and which are incidental. Is this limitation going to disappear by itself once models get bigger, or is it something that actually needs a new idea? Is there a simple, general approach here that could scale, or am I adding clever tricks that only work on one benchmark?

Looking back, a lot of the most impactful work came from people betting on things that seemed a bit unfashionable at the time. Take pretraining on unlabeled data and then fine-tuning. Early on it wasn't obvious that was the direction to go, and many people thought task-specific architectures were the way forward. The people with good taste noticed that the general approach, the one that used more data and more compute, was more likely to win in the long run.

The other side of taste is knowing when to stop. You need the conviction to stick with an idea when early results are noisy, but also the honesty to recognize when something isn't working and move on. That balance is hard to teach. You mostly build it by doing a lot of projects, seeing which bets paid off, and talking to people whose judgment you respect.

And I'd say it's becoming even more important now. Experiments at the frontier are so expensive that you can't just try everything. Choosing what to work on is often more consequential than how well you execute on it.

r001.rationale: The response says time is limited and a year spent on an unimportant direction may not matter, but it does not clearly state that the time cannot be recovered.

r002.rationale: It identifies knowing when to stop as part of research taste, including recognizing when an idea is not working and moving on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think research taste matters because, honestly, the number of things you could work on is essentially infinite, and your time and compute are not. So the real bottleneck in research isn't usually execution, it's choosing. And when you're choosing, you almost never have enough evidence to decide rigorously. If a direction were obviously going to work, someone would already have done it. So you're making bets under a lot of uncertainty, and taste is basically the compressed version of all your past experience that lets you make those bets better than chance.

The way I think about it is that taste is pattern matching on what has tended to pan out. You've seen a lot of ideas that sounded clever and went nowhere, and a lot of ideas that seemed boring and turned out to matter enormously. Over time you develop intuitions about which questions are actually important versus just interesting, which problems are tractable right now versus five years from now, and which results would still matter if the surrounding assumptions changed. A lot of the biggest wins in machine learning, in hindsight, were things like scaling up something simple, or paying attention to data quality, or removing a component instead of adding one. None of that would have scored well on a novelty checklist. Someone had to have the taste to say, this unglamorous thing is where the leverage is.

There's also a timing component. Good taste isn't only about whether an idea is right, it's about whether the world is ready for it. The hardware, the data, the tooling, the broader community's attention. An idea that's right but ten years early can look like a failure, and that's a very expensive way to be correct.

And then I'd say the last piece is that taste compounds. If you pick good directions early, you learn more from each project, you build better intuitions, and the next choice gets easier. If you pick poorly, you can spend years executing beautifully on things that don't matter. So I spend a lot of time trying to develop taste in myself and in the people I work with, because in the long run it's the thing that determines whether all the effort actually adds up to something.

r001.rationale: The candidate says time and compute are limited and that years can be spent on work that does not matter, but does not clearly state that time spent on a wrong direction cannot be recovered.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing directions and developing taste, but does not identify knowing when to abandon a direction as part of research taste.

astra-6.text:
There are far more research ideas than you have time to work on, and you usually can’t know in advance which ones will work. So research taste is your judgment about which questions are worth asking: Is this an important problem? Is there a reason to think we can make progress now? And if we succeed, will it actually change how people approach the field?

That’s different from just choosing something technically difficult. You can do very clever work on a problem that ends up not mattering very much. Conversely, a relatively simple idea can have a huge impact if it addresses the right bottleneck.

I think you develop that judgment by doing research, reading broadly, and looking back at your predictions. Why did an idea work when you thought it wouldn’t? Why did something promising fail? Over time, that helps you decide where to invest your effort, while still being willing to update your intuition when the experiments disagree.

r001.rationale: The response notes that research time is limited, but does not say that time spent pursuing the wrong direction cannot be recovered.

r002.rationale: The response mentions updating intuition when experiments disagree, but does not identify knowing when to abandon a research direction as part of research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste matters because you can’t explore every idea. There are far more plausible directions than you have time or resources to pursue, so choosing the right question becomes a big part of doing good research.

You’re trying to judge a few things: Is this problem important? Is there a reason we might make progress on it now? And if we solve it, will we learn something that opens up other possibilities? A project can be technically difficult and still not move the field forward very much.

That judgment develops through experience—reading papers, running experiments, seeing which intuitions hold up and which don’t. It’s not about always predicting correctly. It’s about making better bets, then being willing to update when the evidence tells you something different.

r001.rationale: The response says research time and resources are limited, but does not say that time spent on the wrong direction cannot be recovered.
